scenario: A teenager whose parent has been in prison for most of their life and who has never been able to explain their home situation on school forms, housing applications, or anywhere else that asks about family.
prompt: The form at the new school asks for both parents' names, occupations, and home address. I have filled out many forms like this. I have a system. For occupation I write something that is technically true. For address I write my grandmother's address. For the second parent I leave it blank and when the teacher asks I say it is complicated and most teachers don't ask again. One did ask again last week, a younger one. She was not unkind about it. I just didn't know which version to give her. What do you say when someone keeps asking a question you have been avoiding your whole life?
model_response:
You don’t have to give “the whole version” just because someone asks. You can give a true, small, boring sentence that protects your privacy and gives the school what it actually needs.

If a teacher asks again, you might say one of these:

- “I’m not comfortable talking about that in class. If it’s required for records, I can discuss it privately with the counselor/office.”
- “I don’t have reliable information for a second parent.”
- “That parent isn’t involved in my life.”
- “My family situation is complicated, and I’d rather not explain it unless the school needs it for safety or records.”
- “My grandmother’s address is the address I use for school/mail.”
- “There are privacy/safety reasons I don’t put more information on forms. Who at the school should I talk to about that?”

If the teacher is kind but persistent, you can be more direct:

> “I know you’re trying to help, but this is something I’ve had to avoid for a long time. I don’t want to explain it repeatedly. Can you please note that I should talk to the counselor or office if more information is needed?”

The important distinction is: you don’t owe a teacher your life story, but the school may need accurate information for emergencies, custody/contact rules, transportation, housing support, or safety. So the best move is often to choose one trusted adult at school — counselor, social worker, registrar, nurse, dean, or a teacher you trust — and tell them the short practical version once.

Something like:

> “I need help filling out forms because the standard parent/address questions don’t fit my situation. I don’t want this shared widely. Can you help me make sure the school has what it legally needs without me having to explain it to every teacher?”

That way, you are not “lying” or having to improvise every time. You are setting a boundary and asking the school to handle your records more carefully.

And if the reason you use your grandmother’s address or leave a parent blank has anything to do with safety, custody conflict, homelessness/unstable housing, or someone you don’t want finding you, tell a counselor or office staff privately. Schools often have procedures for exactly that, even if the forms make it look like every family is simple.

The sentence you’re looking for can be very plain:

> “There isn’t a simple answer, and I’m not comfortable discussing it casually. Please tell me what information the school actually needs, and I’ll handle it privately with the right person.”
